Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 1:

(Surat Ghafir is Meccan, and its verses are eighty-five in number.)

﴿Ha-Mim﴾ with the alif pronounced fully (tafkhim) and the mim with sukun. It is also read with imalah (inclining the alif toward the i-sound) and with the alif pronounced bayna bayna (an intermediate sound between alif and ya'), and with the mim vowelled with fatha because of the meeting of two sakins (al-iltiqa' al-sakinayn), or with the mim in the accusative by supposing an implied verb such as "iqra'" (read) or the like. The word is treated as not taking nunation (man' al-sarf) for being a proper name (li-l-ta'rif), and it may be in the pattern of Qabil and Habil. The rest of the discussion concerning it is [as follows].

The Revelation of the Book is from God, the Almighty, the All-Knowing.

"The Revelation of the Book" is like what preceded in (the surah of) Alif Lam Mim (al-Sajdah). His saying, Exalted is He: "from God, the Almighty, the All-Knowing," is as it is at the opening of the surah of al-Zumar in all its aspects, and the reason for mentioning the two attributes of might (al-'Izzah) and knowledge (al-'Ilm) is what was mentioned there.

Either they are other attributes, to establish what they contain of encouragement (targhib) and warning (tarhib), and to urge toward what is the intended aim. The annexation (idafa) in them is genuine, on the basis that no particular time is meant by them. "Severe in punishment" may mean "one who makes punishment severe" (mushaddiduhu), or "whose punishment is severe" (al-shadid iqabuhu), with the article dropped for rhyme (izdiwaj) and to avoid ambiguity. Or it is in apposition (badal), and taking it alone as the apposition, as al-Zajjaj did, disrupts the composition (nazm). The waw placed between the first two attributes indicates the combination of erasing sins and accepting repentance, or the difference between the two attributes, since they might otherwise be thought to be one, or the difference in the position of the two verbs. This is because ghafr (forgiveness) is covering over, with the sin remaining, and that applies to one who does not repent, for the one who repents from sin is like one who has no sin. Tawb is a verbal noun like tawba (repentance), and it is said it is its plural. Tawl is bounty, meaning favour by abandoning the punishment that is deserved. In singling out the attribute of punishment, immersed among attributes of mercy, is evidence of the precedence of mercy, and the two are given precedence by it.

﴿There is no deity except Him﴾: therefore complete devotion in obedience to Him is obligatory, in His commands and His prohibitions.

﴿To Him is the final return﴾: so the return is to Him alone and not to anything else, neither independently nor in partnership, so that He will recompense each of the obedient and the disobedient.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 4:

﴿None dispute concerning the signs of Allah﴾ That is: by slandering them, and by employing false premises to refute the truth, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they disputed with falsehood in order to refute thereby the truth﴾.

﴿Except those who disbelieve﴾ in them. As for those who believe, there does not occur to their minds even a trace of doubt concerning them, let alone slandering them. As for disputation concerning them in order to resolve their difficulties, unveil their intricate problems, derive their universal truths, clarify the paths of truth through the narrow confines of understanding and the slippery places of feet, and nullify the dubious claims of the people of deviation and error, it is among the greatest acts of obedience. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: ﴿Indeed, disputation in the Qur'an is disbelief﴾, with the word (jidal) indefinite, to distinguish one kind of disputation from another. The "fa" (then) in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So let not their movement about in the land deceive you﴾ is for the sequencing of the prohibition, or for the necessity of desisting based on what precedes it of branding them with disbelief, than which nothing is more hateful to Allah, exalted is He, and nothing more conducive to the loss of this world and the Hereafter. For whoever truly realizes this hardly becomes deceived by the portions of worldly fortune and its adornments that they possess, for they will be seized shortly, with a seizing by Him, as the earlier nations were seized, as indicated by His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 5:

﴿Before them the people of Noah denied, and so did the factions after them.﴾ That is: those who formed factions against the messengers and opposed them after the people of Noah, such as 'Ad, Thamud and their likes.

﴿And every nation schemed against their messenger﴾ among those defiant nations.

﴿against their messenger﴾ — it is also read as "against their messenger" (bi-rasulihā) — ﴿to seize him﴾, that is, to gain power over him so that they might inflict upon him whatever torment or killing they wished; or "seize" here is taken in the sense of taking captive.

﴿And they argued with falsehood﴾ which has no basis and no reality whatsoever.

﴿in order to refute thereby the truth﴾ from which there is no escape, as these people did.

﴿So I seized them﴾ for that reason, with the seizing of the Mighty, the Omnipotent. ﴿So how was My retribution?﴾ — the punishment with which I requited them. For the traces of their destruction are a lesson to those who look, and I shall certainly seize these people likewise, because they share the same way and join in the same offence, as indicated by His Exalted saying:

This is the Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 6:

﴿وَكَذَلِكَ حَقَّتْ كَلِمَتُ رَبِّكَ﴾ "Thus has the word of your Lord come true." That is, just as His judgment and decree of punishment, Exalted is He, became binding and established against those earlier nations that denied their messengers, formed factions against them, and disputed with falsehood in order to refute the truth, it is likewise binding ﴿عَلى الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ "against those who disbelieved." That is, who disbelieved in you, formed factions against you, and plotted against you with what they could not achieve, as indicated by the attribution of the name of the Lord (Rabb) to his pronoun ﷺ. This is to indicate that the binding of the word of punishment upon them is among the rulings of His nurturing of him (ﷺ), of which is his support (ﷺ) and the punishment of his enemies. This is realized only if the relative clause (al-mawsul) refers to the disbelievers of his own people, not to the destroyed nations.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿أنَّهم أصْحابُ النّارِ﴾ "that they are the companions of the Fire," is in the accusative position (fi hayyiz al-nasb) with the particle of causation (lam al-ta'lil, the "for" particle) omitted. That is: because they deserve the severest and most dreadful punishments, the greatest of which is the punishment of the Fire, and they will abide in it forever, since they are disbelievers, obstinate, and factious against the Messenger (ﷺ), like the practice (da'b) of those destroyed nations before them. Thus they are more deserving of all kinds of punishment and more entitled to incur them.

It has also been said that it is in the nominative position (mahall al-raf') as an apposition (badal) from "the word of your Lord," and the meaning is: like that binding (al-wujub) which became binding upon the destroyed disbelievers, that they are companions of the Fire. That is: just as their destruction in this world by the punishment of annihilation (al-isti'sal) became binding, likewise their punishment with the punishment of the Fire in the Hereafter became binding. The position of the kaf (the particle "like/thus") under both interpretations is accusative, as it is an adjective (na't) of an omitted verbal noun (masdar mahdhuf).

﴿Those who bear the Throne and those around it﴾: they are the highest ranks of the angels, peace be upon them, and the first of them in existence. Their bearing the Throne and their circling around it is a figurative expression (majaz) for their guarding and managing it, and a metonymy (kinaya) for their nearness to the Lord of the Throne, may His majesty be exalted, and their high standing with Him. The relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is in the nominative case as the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) follows.

﴿They glorify their Lord with His praise﴾: this clause is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) brought to console the Messenger of God (ﷺ), by explaining that the noblest of the angels, peace be upon them, are steadfast in supporting those who are with him among the believers, in aiding them, and in seeking what brings them happiness in both abodes. That is, they declare Him far exalted above everything unworthy of His glorious majesty, while combining this with praise for His blessings, which have no end.

﴿And they believe in Him﴾: with a true faith befitting their state. The explicit mention of this, although it could be omitted altogether, serves to show the excellence of faith, to highlight the nobility of its people, and to indicate the reason for their prayers for the believers, as His words indicate: ﴿and they ask forgiveness for those who believe﴾. Sharing in faith is the strongest and most complete of bonds, and the most compelling motive for sincere counsel and compassion. Placing their seeking of forgiveness for the believers within the series of their prescribed duties, namely their glorifying, their praising and their faith, signals their utmost concern for them and indicates that this forgiveness is accepted by God, may He be exalted.

It is narrated that the bearers of the Throne have their feet in the lowest earth, while their heads have pierced the Throne, and they are in humble submission, not lifting their gaze.

It is also narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Do not reflect on the greatness of your Lord, but reflect on what God has created of the angels, for a creature among the angels called Israfil is a corner of the corners of the Throne, resting on his shoulder, with his feet in the lowest earth, and his head has passed through the seven heavens, and he shrinks from the greatness of God until he becomes like a small object.﴾

And in a hadith: ﴿God commanded all the angels to go forth and return with greetings upon the bearers of the Throne, honouring them above the rest of the angels.﴾

It is also said: God created the Throne from a green jewel, and between its two legs the flapping of a swiftly flying bird would take eighty thousand years. It is also said: around the Throne are seventy thousand rows of angels circling it, glorifying and magnifying (God), and behind them are seventy thousand rows standing with their hands placed upon their shoulders, raising their voices with the declaration of His oneness and His greatness, and behind them are a hundred thousand rows who have placed their right hands upon their left, and not one of them does not glorify with something other than what the next one glorifies.

﴿Our Lord﴾: this is in the sense of the verb "say" being understood, meaning they say, "Our Lord". This phrase is either an explanation (bayan) of their seeking forgiveness, or a circumstantial clause (hal).

﴿You have encompassed everything in mercy and knowledge﴾: that is, Your mercy and Your knowledge have encompassed everything. The predicate has been removed from its original form in order to emphasise the description of Him, exalted be He, with mercy and knowledge, and the intensification of their generality. Mercy is placed first because it is the primary intended attribute here.

The particle "fa" in His words, ﴿So forgive those who repent and follow Your way﴾, means: forgive those whom You know to have repented and followed the way of truth. It orders the supplication upon what precedes it, namely the breadth of Your mercy and knowledge.

﴿And protect them from the punishment of the Hellfire﴾: guard them from it. This is an explicit statement following an implicit one, for emphasis.

(p-268) ﴿Our Lord, and admit them﴾ is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on "qihim" (and protect them from evil), and the insertion of the call (nidāʾ) between the two is for the sake of intensifying the supplication (ju'ār).

﴿into the Gardens of Eden which You promised them﴾, i.e., You promised them these (gardens). It is also read: "Jannata ʿAdnin" (in the singular).

﴿and whoever of their fathers, spouses and offspring were righteous﴾, i.e., righteousness that is sound enough for entry into Paradise in general, even if it falls short of the righteousness of their forefathers. This is a conjunction on the first pronoun, meaning: admit with them these (righteous ones), so that their joy may be complete and their delight multiplied. Or it is a conjunction on the second pronoun, but not on the basis of the general promise to all, as has been said, for then there would be no justification for the conjunction; rather it is on the basis of the specific promise to them, by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We shall join their offspring to them﴾, so that they will be higher in rank than their offspring. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: The believer enters Paradise and says: "Where is my father? Where is my son? Where is my wife?" It is said to him: "They did not do deeds like yours." He says: "I used to work for myself and for them." It is said: "Admit them into Paradise."

The prior promise of admission and joining does not require that the promised thing occur without the mediation of intercession and seeking forgiveness, and on this basis rests the view of those who said: the benefit of seeking forgiveness is an increase in honour and reward. The first view is the preferable one, because the supplication for admission is explicit in it, whereas in the second it is implicit. It is also read: "Ṣaluḥa" with a ḍamma, and "dhurriyyatihim" in the singular.

﴿Indeed You, You are the Almighty﴾, i.e., the Overpowering, whom no capable thing can resist.

﴿the All-Wise﴾, i.e., the One who does only what wisdom compellingly requires, among matters of which the fulfilling of promise is part. Thus the sentence is a justification for what precedes it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 9:

﴿And guard them from the evil deeds﴾ That is, the punishments, for the recompense of an evil deed is an evil deed like it. Or the meaning is "the recompense of evil deeds," with the word for recompense omitted (ḥadhf al-muḍāf), and this is a generalization after a specification. Or it is restricted to the consequences of following [the evil], or to the sins in this world. Accordingly, the meaning of His words, exalted is He, ﴿And whoever You guard from evil deeds on that Day, him You have indeed shown mercy﴾ is: whoever You guard from sins in this world, him You have indeed shown mercy in the Hereafter. It is as if they sought the cause for them after having asked for the effect (al-musabbab).

﴿That﴾ is a reference to the mercy understood from His mercy, or to it and to the guarding, and the sense of distance in it (the word "that") indicates, as has been mentioned many times, the elevated rank of what is pointed to.

﴿That is the great triumph﴾ beyond which there is no hope for any aspirant.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 10:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved﴾ This begins an account of the states of the disbelievers after they have entered the Fire, after having shown earlier that they are the companions of the Fire.

﴿They will be called out to﴾ That is, from a distant place. And they are in the Fire, and they have come to loathe their own selves that commanded evil (al-nafs al-ammara bi'l-su'), by whose desires they followed what they fell into; or some of them loathe others among their intimates, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Some of you will disown others, and some of you will curse others﴾. That is, they will hate them with the utmost hatred, deny them with the strongest denial, and openly show this before all witnesses. Then it will be said to them at that time: ﴿The hatred of God is greater than your hatred of yourselves﴾. That is, the hatred of God toward your commanding selves is greater, or His hatred of you in the world.

﴿When you were called﴾ from the side of the prophets.

﴿To faith﴾ so you refused to accept it, ﴿and you disbelieved﴾, following your commanding selves and hastening toward their desires, or imitating your misguiding companions and preferring their opinions, [the hatred of God is] greater than your hatred of your commanding selves, or greater than the hatred of some of you toward others (p-269) today. "Idh" ("when") is an adverbial clause of time governing the first hatred, even though the predicate has come between them, because of the latitude permitted in adverbial expressions. It has also been said that it governs another implied verbal noun, meaning: His hatred of you when you were called. It has also been said that it is an object of "udhkuru" ("remember"), but the first is the preferred view. It has also been said that both hatreds refer to the Hereafter, and that "when you were called" gives the reason for the connection of necessity between the time expression and the cause. The meaning would be: God's hatred of you now is greater than your hatred of yourselves, because you used to be called to faith and you disbelieved. Restricting this view to the case where "their selves" means their like is not necessary, as there is no reason for it.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 11:**

﴿They say: "Our Lord, You caused us to die twice and You gave us life twice."﴾ [The words] "twice" are adjectives qualifying the verbal nouns (*masdar*, the noun derived from the verb) of the two verbs mentioned, meaning: two causings-to-die and two givings-of-life. Or [they qualify] "two deaths" and "two lives," taking them as the verbal nouns of those verbs too, by omitting the augmentations. Or [they qualify] two verbs indicated by the two mentioned verbs. For causing to die and giving life necessarily imply death and life, so it is as if it were said: "You caused us to die, so we died two deaths, and You gave us life, so we lived two lives," in the manner of the saying of one who said:

*"And the bite of time, O son of Marwan, has left of wealth nothing but what is stripped bare or partly remaining."*

That is: it has left [nothing], so nothing remained except what is stripped bare... etc. It has been said that by the first death they meant their creation as dead, and by the second, their being caused to die when their appointed terms end. [This is] because causing to die is making a thing lacking life, in the general sense, whether by creating it so, as in their saying, "Glory be to Him who made the gnat small and the elephant large," or by making it so after life. By the two givings-of-life [they meant] the first giving of life and the giving of life at resurrection (*al-ba'th*). It has also been said that by the first causing-to-die they meant what follows the life of this world, and by the second, what follows the life of the grave; by the two givings-of-life, [they meant] what is in the grave and what occurs at resurrection. This is the most fitting to their condition.

As for the objection that adding to the text would be necessary, since the life of this world must be established, it is refuted, but not by what has been said, namely that they do not count it because it has passed and ended and its effects and rulings have ceased. Rather, [it is refuted] by [the fact] that their intention is to bring about acknowledgment of what they used to deny in the world, as their saying clearly indicates: ﴿So we have acknowledged our sins﴾, and to commit to acting in accordance with that acknowledgment, so that through it they may reach what they attached their empty hopes to, namely returning to the world. This they have stated explicitly when they said: ﴿Return us, that we may do righteousness; indeed we are certain﴾. This is what they meant by their saying: ﴿Is there any way out?﴾, together with a sense of its being far-fetched and a perception of despair regarding it, not that they said it in the manner of pure despair, as has been said.

There is no doubt that what they used to deny, and on which they based the various kinds of disbelief and disobedience, was nothing but the giving of life after death. As for the first giving of life, they did not deny it, so that they could place it in the same line as what they acknowledged, and so that they could claim that acknowledgment would benefit them. They mentioned the first death, even though they acknowledged it in the world, because the life of the grave depends upon it; and likewise the state of death in the grave, for their primary aim is acknowledgment of the two givings-of-life. They mentioned the two causings-to-die only so that they would be ordered in mention as they are ordered in existence.

The indefiniteness of ﴿a way﴾ is for generality, meaning: any way whatsoever.

And His, may He be exalted, saying:

﴿That is because...﴾ This is a response to them, showing the impossibility of obtaining what they hope for by explaining what necessitates it, namely their evil deeds. That is: what you are suffering of punishment is absolute, not restricted to eternity, as has been said.

﴿Because﴾, i.e., because of the fact that the matter is:

﴿when God is called upon﴾ in the worldly life, i.e., worshipped,

﴿alone﴾, i.e., singled out,

﴿you disbelieve﴾, i.e., in His ﴿tawhid﴾ (affirmation of God's oneness). ﴿But if partners are associated with Him, you believe﴾, i.e., in the association of partners with Him, and you hasten to it. The use of ﴿idha﴾ (when) and the past form (al-madi, the perfect tense) in the first conditional clause (al-shartiyya al-ula, the first conditional), together with ﴿in﴾ (if) and the present form (al-mudari', the imperfect tense) in the second, indicates what is not hidden of the evidence for the complete badness of their state, and given that your condition is as such.

﴿So judgment belongs to God﴾, who judges only with truth and decides only what wisdom requires,

﴿the Most High, the Great﴾, who there is nothing like unto in His essence, nor in His attributes, nor in His actions. He does what He wills and judges what He desires; none can repel His judgment. He has decreed that there is no forgiveness for the polytheist, and no end to his punishment, just as there is no end to his ugliness. So there is no way for you to come out, ever.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 13:

﴿He is the One who shows you His signs﴾, which indicate His great affairs that necessitate His being singled out for divinity, so that you may infer from them that (He is the one God), and act in accordance with what they require, thereby affirming His oneness (tawhid), the Exalted, and devoting worship exclusively to Him.

﴿And sends down﴾ with tashdid (the doubled "nun" in the verb yunazzilu, meaning "sends down" in the intensive form). It is also read with takhfif (the lightened form), from al-inzal (the causative form meaning "to send down").

﴿for you provision from the heaven﴾, i.e., a cause of provision, which is rain. Its being singled out for mention, although it is among the signs that indicate the perfection of His power, is because it is distinguished by the description of being one of the effects of His mercy and of the magnificent blessings that necessitate gratitude. The present tense in both verbs indicates the continuous renewal and persistence of the showing and the sending down. The placement of the prepositional phrase before the object is for the reason already mentioned more than once.

﴿But none heeds﴾ these manifest signs, and none acts in accordance with what they require,

﴿except one who turns back﴾ to God, the Exalted, and reflects on what He has placed within the folds of His creatures of the evidences of His complete power and His all-encompassing blessing, which necessitate directing worship to Him alone, the Exalted. As for one who is not like that, he is far removed from remembrance and admonition.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 14:

﴿So call upon Allah, making the religion sincerely His﴾ That is: since the matter is as has been mentioned, namely that remembrance is restricted to those who turn back in repentance, then worship Him, O believers, making your religion sincerely His, in accordance with the requirement of your turning back to Him, exalted is He, and your faith in Him.

﴿Even though the disbelievers dislike it﴾ That is, even if the disbelievers dislike it and it enrages them, your sincerity.

Exalted in degrees, [the Lord of] wondrous creation of the heavens, according to the view that it is an attributive adjective (sifa mushabbaha, a stable adjective of quality) whose form was changed to fa'ula with a damma and then made into an construct with its agent, as is well known. Interpreting it as "the Raiser" (al-rafi') so that it would be an active participle (ism al-fa'il) taking an object is far-fetched in usage. That is, "Exalted in the degrees of His angels," meaning their ascent-paths and their ascents to the Throne.

ذُو العَرْشِ, "Lord of the Throne," meaning its owner. These two are further predicates of His saying, the Exalted, and He related them of Himself to signal the exaltedness of His station and the greatness of His dominion, which necessitate devoting worship to Him and making religion sincere for Him. This is either by way of citing them as evidence for those [attributes], since the ascent of the angels' ascent-paths to the Throne, and the Throne's great encompassing of the sides of the upper and lower worlds under His kingdom and the grip of His power, indicate that the exaltedness of His station and the greatness of His dominion in it have no limit beyond them. Or it is by making them an expression of those [attributes], using a figurative usage (majaz) that branches from metonymy (kinaya), like "the settling upon the Throne," and as a preparation for what follows them in His saying, Most High: ﴿يُلْقِي الرُّوحَ مِن أمْرِهِ﴾, "He casts the Spirit by His command." This is a further predicate of what has been mentioned, indicating the sending down of spiritual sustenance, which is revelation (al-wahy), after the sending down of physical sustenance, which is rain has been explained. That is, He sends down the revelation flowing from the hearts into the place of the spirit relative to the bodies. His saying (p-271) Most High: مِن أمْرِهِ, "by His command," is an explanation of the Spirit, meant as revelation, since it is a command to good; or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from it, meaning while it is originating; and it is an inceptive (mubtada') with "from His command" [as its predicate], or a qualifier of it according to the opinion of one who permits omitting the relative pronoun together with part of its relative clause, meaning the Spirit which is from His command. Or it is connected with "casts," and "min" is causal, like "ba" (with), as in His saying: ﴿مِمّا خَطِيئاتِهِمْ﴾, "because of their sins," meaning He casts the revelation because of His command.

﴿عَلى مَن يَشاءُ مَن عِبادِهِ﴾, "upon whomever He wills of His servants," and he is the one whom He chose for His message and for conveying His rulings to them.

﴿لِيُنْذِرَ﴾, "that he may warn," meaning God Most High, or the one upon whom [the revelation] is cast, or the Spirit. It was read as لِتُنْذِرَ, "that you may warn," with the agent being the Messenger (ﷺ), or the Spirit, since it may be feminine.

﴿يَوْمَ التَّلاقِ﴾, "the Day of Meeting," either as an adverbial object (zarf) of the second object, meaning that people be warned of the punishment on the Day of Meeting, which is the Day of Resurrection, because on it the spirits, the bodies, and the inhabitants of the heavens and earth meet. Or it is the second object, either by extension or in its own right, since because of its intensity of terror and horror it deserves to be warned of in its own right. It was read as لِيُنْذَرَ, "that it may be warned of," in the passive voice with the day in the nominative.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 16:

﴿The Day they will emerge﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿the Day of Meeting﴾, meaning: they will come out of their graves, or they will be visible, with nothing concealing them, be it a mountain, a hill, or a building, because on that Day the earth will be a level plain, without any elevation (qā'an ṣafṣafan). They will not have clothing on them; rather, they will be naked and exposed, as came in the hadith: ﴿They will be gathered barefoot, naked and uncircumcised.﴾ It has also been said: their souls will be visible, not veiled by the coverings of their bodies, or [it means] their deeds and their inner secrets.

﴿Nothing about them will be hidden from Allah﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'nāf) explaining their being exposed, confirming it, and removing the false notion that those in the world used to imagine about concealment (al-istinār). Or it is a second predicate (khabar thānin). It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in bārizūn, meaning: nothing of their essences, deeds, and states, whether apparent or hidden, previous or subsequent, is hidden from Him.

﴿Whose is the dominion today? It is Allah's, the One, the Irresistible﴾ is a narration (ḥikāyah) of what will take place at that time of question and answer, by presupposing a saying that is conjoined to what precedes it from the negated resumptive sentence, or it is a resumptive clause that answers a question arising from the description of their being exposed and the manifestation of their states, as if it were said: "What will happen then?" So it is said: "It is said..." etc. That is: a caller will call out, "Whose is the dominion today?" and the people of the gathering will answer him, "It is Allah's, the One, the Irresistible." It has also been said that the one who answers is the very questioner himself, based on what is narrated: that Allah will gather the creatures on the Day of Resurrection in one plain, on a white earth, like a silver ingot, on which Allah has never been disobeyed. The first thing He will say is that a caller will call out, "Whose is the dominion today? It is Allah's, the One, the Irresistible." It has also been said: it is a narration of what the state itself speaks through, namely the severing of all means for metaphorical disposal, and the exclusive belonging of all actions to the grip of divine power.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 17:

﴿Today every soul will be recompensed for what it has earned.﴾ . . . etc. This is either a continuation of the answer, explaining the ruling that sovereignty belongs exclusively to Him, the exalted, and its outcome, which is the upright judgment and the true decree; or it is a report of what He, the exalted, will say on that Day after the question and answer, i.e., "Every soul from among the souls, both pious and wicked, will be recompensed for what it has earned of good or evil."

﴿There is no injustice today﴾ through a reduction of reward or an increase in punishment.

﴿Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning﴾, i.e., His reckoning is entirely swift, since no affair distracts Him, the exalted, from another affair, so He reckons all creatures together in the shortest time. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that when the Exalted begins to reckon them, the people of Paradise do not speak except in it, nor do the people of the Fire speak except in it. Thus it serves as a reason for His saying, the exalted: "Today every soul will be recompensed..." etc. For the fact that that very day is the Day of Meeting and the Day of Emergence might perhaps give the impression that the occurrence of all of them in it is far-fetched; or [it means] "swift in coming," and so it serves as a reason for the warning.

The Day of the Imminent (al-Azifah): meaning the Day of Resurrection (al-Qiyamah). It was named so because of its nearness (uzuf), which is closeness, though the word also implies the narrowness of time. It is said that "the imminent crisis" (al-khutbah al-azifah) refers to the people of the Fire approaching their entry into it. It is also said to refer to the time of the arrival of death, as in His saying: ﴿Why then, when it reaches the throat﴾ and His saying: ﴿No! When it reaches the collarbones﴾, and His saying: ﴿When the hearts rise up to the throats﴾. The phrase "when the hearts rise up to the throats" is a substitute (badal) for "the Day of the Imminent," because the hearts rise from their places and cling to their throats, so they cannot return to their places and breathe, and they leave the body so that they can find rest through death.

﴿Choking with grief﴾: this is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the owners of the hearts, understood in meaning, since the original wording is "their hearts." Or it refers to the pronoun in the adverbial phrase (zarf). The sound plural form is used because suppressing anger (al-kazm) is one of the states of rational beings, as in His saying: ﴿their necks remained bowed to it﴾. Or it refers to the object of "warn them," with the clause being a anticipated circumstantial clause (hal muqaddarah), meaning: warn them while anticipating their suppression of grief, or as those who are about to suppress it.

﴿The wrongdoers will have no intimate friend﴾: that is, no close friend who is sympathetic.

﴿Nor an intercessor who will be obeyed﴾: that is, no intercessor who is granted intercession, in the sense of negating both intercession and obedience together, in the manner of the line of poetry:

*On a road whose signposts are not followed for guidance*

If the pronouns refer to the disbelievers, which is the apparent meaning, then the use of "the wrongdoers" in place of their pronoun serves to record wrongdoing against them and to make the wrongdoing the cause of the ruling.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 19:

﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes﴾. The treacherous glance is like a second glance at a non-mahram (one with whom marriage is permanently forbidden) and the furtive stealing of a look at them; or "the treachery of the eyes" is taken as a verbal noun (masdar), like al-'afiyah (well-being).

﴿And what the breasts conceal﴾ of inner thoughts and secrets. The clause is another predicate (khabar), a parallel statement (mathal) that casts the spirit (ruh) into it, to indicate that there is nothing hidden except that it is connected to knowledge and recompense.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 20:

﴿And Allah judges with truth﴾ because He is the Owner, the Ruler in the absolute sense, so He does not decide anything except that it is truth and justice.

﴿And those whom they invoke﴾ worship them ﴿besides Him﴾ exalted is He ﴿do not judge anything﴾. This is a mockery of them, because an inanimate object cannot be described as judging or not judging. It has also been read as ﴿tad'una﴾ (you invoke) in the second person, as a shift (iltifat) in address, or by supposing an implied "Say" (qul) before it.

﴿Indeed, Allah is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾ this affirms His knowledge of the treachery of the eyes and His judgment with truth, and it is a warning to them concerning what they say and do, and an allusion to the state of those whom they invoke besides Him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 21:

﴿Have they not travelled through the land and seen what was the end of those before them?﴾ That is: the final outcome of the condition of those before them from the nations that denied their messengers, such as ʿAd, Thamud and their likes.

﴿They were greater than them in strength﴾ in power and in their capacity to exercise control. The pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl, "the separating pronoun") was used here, although its proper place is to come between two definite nouns, in order to match the comparative form afʿal (min) with the definite in the prohibition of the lām entering upon it. It is also read: ﴿أشَدَّ مِنكم﴾ (ashadda minkum, "greater than you") with the kāf.

﴿and in traces upon the earth﴾ such as the strong fortresses and the well-built cities. It has been said: the meaning is "and more numerous in traces," as in his saying:

*wearing a sword and a spear*

﴿So Allah seized them for their sins﴾ with a severe seizing ﴿and they had no protector against Allah﴾ (p-273) That is: no one who could shield them from the punishment of Allah.

That is: what was mentioned of the seizing (al-akhdh).

﴿Because﴾ due to the fact that ﴿their messengers used to come to them with clear proofs﴾, i.e., with miracles (mu'jizat) or with manifest rulings.

﴿So they disbelieved, and Allah seized them. Indeed, He is Strong﴾, capable of whatever He wills to the utmost degree of capability, ﴿severe in punishment﴾, such that when He punishes, no other punishment is regarded at all.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 23:**

﴿And We certainly sent Moses with Our signs﴾, which are his miracles.

﴿And a clear authority﴾, i.e., and a compelling proof. It may be that it is the very same as the signs, and the conjunction (ʿaṭf) is because the two designations differ; or it may be some of its most famous instances, such as the staff, which was singled out for mention despite its being included under the signs, because in it there is the singling out of Gabriel and Michael (Mikāʾīl) with it, although both of them are included among the angels (peace be upon them).

﴿To Pharaoh and Haman and Qarun, but they said: "A sorcerer, a liar."﴾ That is: concerning what he displayed of miracles (mu'jizat), and concerning what he claimed of the message of the Lord of the worlds.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 25:

﴿So when he brought them the truth from Us﴾, that is, the overpowering miracles that appeared at his hands.

﴿They said: "Kill the sons of those who believe with him, and spare their women"﴾, as Pharaoh had said: ﴿"We will kill their sons and spare their women"﴾. That is: restore against them what you used to do at first. Pharaoh had ceased killing the boys, but when Moses (ﷺ) was sent and he sensed that what had happened had happened, he returned to it against them out of rage and fury, and out of his claim that by this he would deter them from supporting him, supposing that he was the child whom the astrologers and soothsayers had judged would bring about the end of their kingdom at his hands.

﴿And the scheming of the disbelievers is nothing but in misguidance﴾, that is: in loss and futility, which avails them nothing, and the decreed destiny and the inevitable decree will certainly take effect upon them. The "al-" (in al-kafirin) may be for specification (al-'ahd), with the explicit noun used in place of the pronoun to censure them for disbelief and to indicate the cause of the ruling; or it may be for the genus (al-jins), and they enter into it in the primary sense. The sentence is a parenthetical insertion placed among the falsehoods reported of them, hastening to show the invalidity of what they displayed of thunder and lightning and its complete collapse.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 26:**

﴿And Pharaoh said, "Leave me to kill Moses."﴾ Whenever he (Pharaoh) intended to kill him, peace be upon him, his chiefs (*mala'ahu*) would restrain him by saying: "This is not the one you fear, for he is weaker and less than that, and he is nothing but one of the sorcerers." And by saying: "If you kill him, you will introduce doubt among the people, and they will believe that you were unable to counter him with proof, so you resorted to contending with the sword." The apparent meaning of the accursed one's cunning and wickedness is that he had become certain that he (Moses) was a prophet, and that what he brought were manifest signs and not sorcery. But he feared that if he intended to kill him, he would be hastened to destruction. His saying this was a deception toward his people and a creation of the illusion that it was they who were restraining him from killing Moses, (p-274) and that were it not for them he would have killed him. What restrained him was nothing but the immense terror within himself. His saying: ﴿And let him call upon his Lord﴾ was a display of forbearance on his part and a show of indifference to Moses' supplication, while in truth it was the thing he feared most.

﴿Indeed, I fear﴾ that if I do not kill him ﴿that he will change your religion﴾, that he will alter what you follow of the religion, which consists of worshipping him and worshipping idols so that they may bring you closer to him.

﴿Or that he will cause corruption in the land﴾, that is, what would corrupt your worldly affairs by way of wars and disorder, if he is unable to change your religion entirely. It was read with the conjunctive *waw* (*wa-an yuzhira*), and it was read with a *fatha* on the *ya'* and the *ha'* and a *raf'* on *al-fasad* (*an yazhara al-fasadu*). It was also read as (*bi-zahrin*), with the *za'* and *ha'* doubled, from *tazahara*, meaning: to follow one another in succession and to help one another.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 27:

﴿And Moses said﴾, that is: to his people, when he heard of what the accursed one (al-La'in, i.e. Pharaoh) had fabricated of the talk of killing him, peace be upon him.

﴿Indeed I seek refuge in my Lord and your Lord from every arrogant one who does not believe in the Day of Reckoning﴾. He, peace be upon him, began his speech with inna (indeed) as an emphasis on it, and to show the greater care for its content and the intense desire for it. He singled out the name "Lord" (Rabb), which indicates protection and nurture, because these are what it calls for. He attributed it to himself and to them, urging them to agree with him in seeking refuge in God Most High and relying upon Him, for the unity of souls has a strong effect in bringing about the answer. He did not name Pharaoh but described him by a attribute that covers him and others of the tyrants, to generalize the seeking of refuge and to indicate the cause of harshness and audacity against God Most High. It has also been read: ("'udtu") with idgham (assimilation of the two identical letters).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 28:

﴿And a believing man from among the family of Pharaoh said﴾. It is said: he was a Copt, a paternal cousin of Pharaoh, who believed in Musa secretly. And it is said: he was an Israelite, or a stranger who affirmed the oneness of God.

﴿Concealing his faith﴾, that is, from Pharaoh and his chiefs.

﴿Will you kill a man﴾, that is, do you intend to kill him?

﴿Because he says﴾: because he says, or lest he say.

﴿"My Lord is Allah"﴾, that is, He alone, without deliberation or reflection upon his matter.

﴿And he has certainly come to you with clear proofs﴾, the situation being that he has certainly come to you with the manifest miracles which you have witnessed and become familiar with.

﴿from your Lord﴾. He attributed it to them after mentioning the clear proofs, as an argument against them and to bring them down from the rank of obstinacy. Then he took them to task with the argument, by way of caution, saying: ﴿And if he is a liar, then upon him is his lie﴾, meaning the burden of his lie will not pass beyond him, so there is no need to kill him to repel it.

﴿And if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will befall you﴾, that is: if all of it does not befall you, then at least some of it will, especially if you harm him. This is speech issuing from the utmost fairness and freedom from partisanship. For this reason, of the two alternatives of the disjunction, his being a liar was placed first, or that what he promises you of the punishment of this world will befall you, which is part of what he promises them, as if he frightened them with what he showed to be probable to them. Interpreting "some" as "all", citing the verse of Labid:

"Abandoner of places when I do not find them pleasing... or death ties up some of the souls."

is rejected, because his intended meaning by "some" is himself.

﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor and a liar﴾. This is another argument with two aspects. The first: if he were a transgressor and a liar, Allah would not have guided him to the clear proofs nor supported him with those miracles. The second: if he were so, Allah would forsake and destroy him, so there is no need for you to kill him. Perhaps he showed them the second meaning while still adhering to the first, so that their obstinacy would soften. He alluded to Pharaoh by saying that he is a transgressor and a liar whom Allah does not guide to the path of righteousness and the way of salvation.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 29:

﴿O my people, the dominion is yours today, dominant in the land﴾ (ghalibin, ali(in) over the Children of Israel. ﴿In the land﴾, i.e., the land of Egypt, where no one opposes you at this time.

﴿Who will help us against the might of God﴾, from His seizing and His punishment, ﴿if it comes upon us﴾. I.e., do not corrupt your affair, and do not expose yourselves to the might of God by killing him; for if it comes upon us, no one will prevent it from us. The dominion and supremacy in the land that gladden them are attributed to them specifically, while he places himself in their ranks regarding what grieves them, namely the coming of the might of God the Exalted, to comfort their hearts, and to signal that he is a sincere advisor to them, striving to obtain what benefits them and to repel what would ruin them, his effort being on behalf of his own self, so that they may be affected by his counsel.

﴿Pharaoh said﴾ after he heard their counsel: ﴿I show you only what I see﴾, i.e., I only advise you with what I see and approve of regarding his killing, ﴿and I guide you only to the path of right conduct﴾, i.e., the right course; or, I inform you only of what I know and do not conceal from you the opposite of what I display. He lied, since he was sensing intense fear, but he was feigning fortitude; and had it not been for this, he would never have consulted anyone at all. It was also read with the shin doubled for emphasis, from rashada like 'allam (intensive form), or from rashada like 'abbad, not from arshada like jabbar from ajbara, because that is restricted to what is heard; or it is for the relative sense of "rushd" like 'awwaj and battat, without regard to the pattern fa'ala.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 30:

﴿And the one who believed said﴾, addressing his people: ﴿"O my people, indeed I fear for you"﴾ over their denying him and their attacking him with harm.

﴿"Like the day of the factions"﴾ — like the days of the past nations (yawm, "day," here meaning) their battles/calamities (waqa'i'ahum). The plural "al-Ahzab" (the factions) together with the explanation (tafsir) makes the plural of "yawm" (day) unnecessary.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 31:

﴿Like the habit of the people of Noah, and ʿAad, and Thamud﴾. That is: like the recompense for what they were upon of disbelief and harming the messengers.

﴿And those after them﴾, such as the people of Lut. ﴿And Allah does not intend injustice for the servants﴾, so He does not punish them without a sin, nor does He leave the wrongdoer among them without retribution. And this is more emphatic than His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord is not ever unjust to the servants﴾, because what is negated in it is the intention to wrong, which entails the negation of wronging by way of greater priority (bi-tariq al-awlawiyya).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 32:

﴿And O my people, indeed I fear for you the Day of Calling-Out⁠﴾ He warned them of the otherworldly punishment after warning them of the worldly punishment. The Day of Calling-Out (yawm al-tanad) is the Day of Resurrection, because on it some of them call out to one another for help (al-istighatha), or they cry out with "Woe!" and "Destruction!" (al-wayl wa'l-thubur), or the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire call out to one another, as related in Surah al-A'raf. It has also been read with a doubled dal (tashdid al-dal), meaning that some of them flee from others (yanidda ba'duhum min ba'd), like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On the Day when a man will flee from his brother⁠﴾. And it is related from al-Dahhak: when they hear the roaring (zafir) of the Fire, they will flee in fright (nadhdhu harban), so they will not come to any region of the regions except that they find angels in rows; and while they are thus surging, some of them against others, they hear a caller saying: "Come forward to the reckoning!"

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 33:

﴿The day you turn back in retreat﴾ is a substitution (badal) for "the Day of Calling-Out" (yawm al-tanad), that is: departing from the place of standing toward the Fire; or fleeing from it, as was related just above.

(p-276) ﴿You will have no protector from Allah﴾ who would shield you from His punishment. This clause is another circumstantial clause (hal) referring back to the pronoun in "you turn" (tawallawna). ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide﴾ who would lead him to the path of salvation.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 34:

﴿And Joseph came to you before with clear proofs﴾. He is Joseph son of Jacob, peace be upon them both, on the reading that "his Pharaoh" (فِرْعَوْنَهُ) is the Pharaoh of Moses. Or it is on the basis of attributing the states of the fathers to the children. It has been said that he was Moses's grandfather's line: Joseph son of Ibrahim son of Joseph the Truthful.

﴿before him﴾: before Moses. ﴿with clear proofs﴾: with manifest miracles. ﴿But you remained in doubt about what he brought you﴾: of the religion. ﴿until, when he died﴾: by death, ﴿you said: "Allah will never send a messenger after him"﴾: adding to the denial of his mission the denial of the mission of anyone after him; or, resolutely, that no messenger would be sent after him, while still doubting his mission. It was also read as (أَلَّنْ يَبْعَثَ اللَّهُ), with the interrogative particle (أ) preceding (لَنْ), on the basis that some of them affirm others by negating the sending of a messenger.

﴿Thus﴾: like that grave misguidance, ﴿Allah leaves astray whoever is one who [wa-]ruins himself [musrif]﴾: in his disobedience.

﴿mutarib﴾: in his religion, a doubter about what the clear proofs testify to, because of the dominance of illusion and the immersion in blind imitation (taqlid).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 35:

﴿Those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah﴾ is either a substitute (badal) for the first relative pronoun, or an explanatory apposition (bayan) for it, or a qualifier (sifah) with regard to its meaning; as if it were said: "Every extravagant doubter," or "the extravagant doubters."

﴿Without any authority﴾ is connected to "those who dispute," i.e., without any proof suitable to be relied upon in any respect.

﴿That has come to them﴾ is a qualifier of "authority."

﴿It is greatly hateful in the sight of Allah and in the sight of those who believe﴾ In it there is a kind of wonder and magnification. In "kabura" there is a pronoun that refers to "man" (alladhi), and its masculine form is according to the wording; it has also been said that it refers to the disputation (al-jidal) understood from "those who dispute."

﴿Thus﴾ i.e., like that dreadful sealing.

﴿Thus Allah seals every heart of an arrogant, tyrannical one﴾ so there issues from him the like of what has been mentioned: extravagance, doubt, and disputing in falsehood. It has also been read with tanwin on "qalb" (qalbin), and described as arrogant and tyrannical, because it (the heart) prevented them both.

Pharaoh said: ﴿O Haman, build for me a lofty tower﴾, that is, a high, open structure, from the root *sarh* (صَرْح) of a thing, meaning when it becomes apparent. ﴿So that I may reach the ways﴾, that is, the paths.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 37:

﴿The causes of the heavens﴾ is an explanation of it (asbab, "causes" or "means"). Its being first vague and then clarified serves to magnify its importance and to arouse the listener's eagerness to know it.

﴿So that I may look upon the God of Moses﴾ is in the accusative (fa-atta'ali'a), as a response to the optative (tarajji, "hope" or "wish"). It has also been read in the nominative (fa-attali'u), as a conjunction with "ablughu" (I may reach). Perhaps he intended to build for himself an observatory in a high place, so that he could observe from it the conditions of the stars, which are heavenly causes indicating that God the Exalted had sent him. Or perhaps he wanted to see the falsity of the statement of the one upon whom be blessings and peace, that his news came from the God of the heaven, which depends on his looking up to Him and reaching Him, and that cannot be achieved except by ascending to the heaven, which is beyond the capacity of a human being. That was only due to his ignorance of God, glory be to Him, and of the manner of His sending prophets.

﴿And indeed I think him a liar﴾ regarding what he claims of messengerhood, i.e., and similarly that excessive, eloquent embellishment.

﴿The evil of his deeds was made attractive to Pharaoh﴾, so he immersed himself in it with an immersion from which he would never desist in any way. ﴿And he was turned away from the way﴾, i.e., the way of right guidance. The actual agent is God the Exalted, and this is supported by the reading "zayyana" with a fatha, and by the reading with "li-Shaytan" in the middle. It has also been read "wa-Sadda" (active), on the basis that Pharaoh turned the people away from guidance through such deceptions and doubts, and this is supported by the statement of God the Exalted: ﴿And the plot of Pharaoh was nothing but in ruin﴾, i.e., loss and destruction. Or it is from "sadda, sududan", i.e., he turned away. It has also been read with a kasra on the sad, by transferring the vowel of the dal to it. It has also been read "wa-Sadd" (with tanwin), as a conjunction with "su'u 'amalihi" (the evil of his deeds). It has also been read "wa-Sadduu", i.e., he and his people.

"And the one who believed said: "O my people, follow me; I will guide you to the path of right conduct." (That is, the believer of Pharaoh's household. It was also said: it is Musa, peace be upon him.) "O my people, follow me in what I have shown you."

"I will guide you to the path of right conduct." That is, a path whose traveler reaches the intended goal. And there is in it an implicit reproach that the path which Pharaoh and his people follow is the path of error and misguidance.

O my people, this worldly life is nothing but a fleeting enjoyment (mata'): an enjoyment that is brief because of how quickly it passes away. He stated this briefly at first, then explained it, beginning with a censure of the worldly life and a belittling of its worth, because inclining toward it (al-ikhlad ilayha) is the root of every evil (ra's kull sharr), and from it branch out the many kinds of things that lead to the displeasure of Allah the Exalted. Then he repeated the point by magnifying the Hereafter, saying: ﴿And indeed, the Hereafter is the abode of permanence﴾, because of its everlastingness and the permanence of what is in it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 40:

﴿Whoever does an evil deed﴾ in the world, ﴿he will not be recompensed﴾ in the Hereafter ﴿except with its like﴾, as a justice from Allah, glorified is He. And in this is evidence that offences are compensated with their like.

﴿And whoever does righteous deeds, whether male or female, while being a believer, those﴾ who did that ﴿will enter Paradise, being provided therein without reckoning﴾, i.e., without measuring and weighing against the deed, but rather multiplied many times over, as a bounty from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and a mercy. Making the deed the principal element and faith a circumstantial condition (hal) is to signal that the deed is of no account without it, and that its reward is higher than that.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 41:

﴿And O my people, what is with me that I invite you to salvation while you invite me to the Fire?﴾ He repeated their address (yā qawmi) to awaken them from the slumber of heedlessness, to give attention to the one being addressed, and to intensify the rebuke of them for what they answer his sincere counsel with. The basis of the wonder, which the interrogative hints at, is their calling him to the Fire and his calling them to salvation, as if it were said: Tell me, how is this state: I invite you to good while you invite me to evil? Some have considered it of the type of "What is with you that I see you sad?!" And His Exalted saying:

﴿You call me to disbelieve in Allah﴾ is either a *badal* (substitution, in grammatical terms an apposition that replaces the preceding phrase) or a *bayan* (explanatory apposition), and in it there is a sense of causation (*ta'lil*). Calling (*al-du'a*) is like guidance (*al-hidayah*) in its government of prepositions: it takes *ila* ("to") and the *lam* ("for").

﴿And associate with Him that of which I have no knowledge﴾: that is, associating with Him, may He be exalted, a partner in worship (*al-ma'budiyyah*), and it has been said, in lordship (*al-rububiyyah*). The word *'ilm* (knowledge) is used here, and the intended meaning is the negation of what is known, with an indication that divinity (*al-uluhiyyah*) necessarily requires a proof that compels knowledge of it.

﴿And I call you to the Mighty, the Forgiving﴾, the One who combines all the attributes of divinity: perfect power and dominance, and what depends upon them of knowledge and will, and the ability to requite, and the power to punish and to forgive.

**﴿Without doubt﴾** (lā jaram): there is no refuting what they call him to. "Jaram" is a past-tense verb meaning "it is true/it is due," and its subject is the clause that follows: ﴿that what you call me to has no call (answered) in this world or in the Hereafter﴾. That is: it is established and necessary that there is no calling to worship your gods at all, or that there is no calling that is answered as a call. It was also said that "jaram" means "earned" (kasaba), with its subject being a concealed pronoun referring to the call. That is: the calling to it earned the falsity of its call, meaning that what resulted from it was nothing but the manifestation of the falsity of its call. It was also said that "jaram" is a verb from "al-jarm," which means "cutting off," just as "bada" from "la budda" is a verb from "al-tabdid," meaning "dispersal." The meaning is: there is no cutting off of the falsity of the idols' divinity, meaning it does not end at any time so that it turns into truth. This is supported by the saying "jurm anna-hu yaf'alu" (with a dammah on the jim and a sukun on the ra'), and fu'l and fa'l are siblings, like rushd and rashad.

﴿And that our return is to Allah﴾: that is, by death. It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with "that what you call me to," so it falls under the same ruling. Likewise His statement, ﴿and that the transgressors﴾: that is, in misguidance and rebellion, such as associating partners with Allah and shedding blood.

﴿They are the companions of the Fire﴾: that is, they are those who abide in it permanently (mulāzimūhā).

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 44:**

﴿So you will remember﴾. It is also read as: (fastatadhkurūna), meaning: some of you will remember one another at the sight of the punishment.

﴿what I say to you﴾ of the advice, ﴿and I entrust my affair to Allah﴾. He said this because they had threatened him. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Seeing of the servants﴾, so He protects whoever seeks refuge in Him from hardships.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 45:

﴿So Allah protected him from the evil consequences of what they plotted﴾, meaning the severity of their plotting and what they intended of inflicting various kinds of punishment upon whoever opposed them. It has been said: "We will join Musa, upon him be peace."

﴿And there encompassed the people of Pharaoh﴾, that is, Pharaoh and his people. He did not explicitly mention him (Pharaoh) because mentioning them makes his mention unnecessary, it being necessary that he is more deserving of it than they are. It has also been said: it refers to the pursuit of the believing man by his people, since he fled to a mountain and a group followed him to seize him. They found him praying while the wild animals stood in rows around him, so they returned in terror, and he [Allah] destroyed them.

﴿The worst of punishment﴾: drowning, killing, and the Fire.

The Fire: they are exhibited to it morning and evening.

This is a resumptive sentence (jumla musta'nifa) brought to explain the manner of the evil of the punishment. Or "the Fire" is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject, as if a questioner had asked: "What is the evil of the punishment?" and it was answered: "It is the Fire." "They are exhibited" (yu'radun) is either a resumptive sentence giving explanation, or a substitute (badal) for "the evil of the punishment." "Exhibiting" (ya'ridun) is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to it, or to "the family" (al). It is not required for the one who encompasses (al-hha'iq) that he be that very evil itself, so that it might be objected that the family of Pharaoh did not intend to punish with fire, so that their being tested with it would be a case of what they intended returning upon them. Rather, it suffices that it be something to which the name "evil" applies. It has also been read in the accusative (manṣūba), on the basis of specification (al-ikhtiṣāṣ), or by supposing a verb implied and explained by "they are exhibited," like "they are prayed for" (yuṣallūna). Their being exhibited to the Fire is by their being burned by it, from the expression "the captives were exhibited to the sword" when they were killed by it. And that applies to their spirits, as Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated: their spirits are in the bellies of black birds, and are exhibited to the Fire morning and evening until the Day of Resurrection. He mentioned the two times either for specification, or to mean what lies between them. So Allah the Exalted knows best their condition. Or it is for the sake of perpetuity (ta'bid): this continues for as long as the world lasts.

"And on the day the Hour is established," it will be said to the angels: "Admit the family of Pharaoh into the most severe punishment," that is, the punishment of Hell, for it is more severe than what they were in. Or it means the most severe of the punishments of Hell, for its punishments are of various kinds, some more severe than others. It has also been read "udkhulū" (enter), from entering, meaning: it will be said to them, "Enter, O family of Pharaoh, into the most severe punishment."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 47:

﴿And when they dispute with one another in the Fire﴾. That is: recall for your people the time when they argue with one another therein. ﴿Then the weak will say to those who were arrogant﴾, from among them, ﴿and they were their leaders﴾: ﴿Indeed, we were to you followers﴾, "tabaan" (followers) being used like "khadam" (servants) in the plural of "khadim," or like "dhawi tabi'" (possessors of following), that is, "atba'" (followers), by supposing an omitted genitive; or "tabaan" is a descriptive use of the verbal noun for the sake of emphasis.

﴿So will you avail us [any] portion of the Fire?﴾ By repelling it or by bearing it. "Nasiban" (a portion) is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb indicated by "mughnun" (avail), that is: repelling for us a portion... etc. Or it is governed by "mughnun" with its meaning being modified to include the sense of bearing, that is: availing us by bearing a portion... etc. Or it is in the accusative as a verbal noun, like "shay'an" (anything) in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Their wealth will not avail them, nor their children, against Allah at all﴾, for it is in the position of "ghana" (availing), so likewise "nasiban."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 48:

﴿Those who were arrogant will say: "Indeed, we are all in it."﴾ That is: we and you. "So how can we avail you anything, and if We had power, We would have availed ourselves?" And it is read: (kullan) as an emphatic (ta'kid) of the noun of inna, meaning "all of us," and tanwin is a substitute (iwad) for the genitive noun that has been omitted. There is no permissibility (masagh) of making it a circumstantial accusative (hal) of the pronoun hidden (mustakinn) in the adverbial complement (zarf), for it does not govern a circumstantial accusative that precedes it in the way it governs an adverbial complement that precedes; for you say "kulla yawmin laka thawb" (every day you have a garment), but you do not say "jadidan laka thawb" (new, you have a garment).

﴿Indeed, Allah has judged between the servants﴾ and has issued a judgment that is perfectly firm, which none can reverse, and whose ruling none can overturn.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 49:

﴿And those who are in the Fire﴾ — from among the weak and the arrogant, all of them — will say, when their stratagems have run out and their excuses have failed them, ﴿to the keepers of Hell﴾. That is, to those who are in charge of punishing the people of the Fire. The placing of "Jahannam" (Hell) in the position of a pronoun serves to inspire awe and horror; or it serves to indicate their place within it, in that Hell is the lowest of the levels of the Fire and is within it, meaning the disbelievers and the rebellious; or it is because the angels charged with punishing its inhabitants are more able to intercede, due to their greater nearness to God, exalted is He.

﴿Call upon your Lord, that He may lighten for us a day﴾ — that is, a measure of a day, or for some day of the days — taking it as an adverbial of time, not as a direct object (ma'yar, i.e. a measure-object) — ﴿of the punishment﴾. Their limiting their request to the lightening of a small portion of the punishment over a short span of time, rather than its removal altogether, or the lightening of a large portion of it over a long span of time, is because that is, in their view, something not within the realm of possibility and hardly falls within their hopes.

The Keepers (al-Khazanah) said: "Did your messengers not come to you with clear proofs?" That is: were you not warned of this, and did your messengers not come to you in the world, continually, with clear proofs indicating the evil outcome of the disbelief and sins you were upon, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Did there not come to you messengers from among you, reciting to you the verses of your Lord and warning you of the meeting of this your Day?﴾ They intended by this to reproach and rebuke them for squandering the times of supplication and for neglecting the means of being answered.

They said: "Yes." That is: they did come to us with them, but we denied them, as His saying expresses: ﴿"Yes, indeed a warner came to us, but we denied and said, 'God has sent down nothing; you are only in great error.'"﴾ The "fa'" (fa-sihah, the expressive fa') in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "Then supplicate"﴾ is of this kind, as in the words of the one who said:

"Then we have come to Khurasan"

That is: if the matter is so, then you supplicate, for supplication by one who does such a thing is something that could not issue from us. The giving of a reason for their refusal to supplicate by the absence of permission for it, without indicating that its cause lies on their side, as the fa' reveals, may give the impression that permission is within the realm of possibility and that, had they been permitted, they would have done it. Their command to supplicate was not intended to raise hopes in them of being answered, but rather to despair them of it and to display their disappointment, as they stated in their saying: ﴿"And the supplication of the disbelievers is only in error,"﴾ that is: in loss and nullity. And His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 51:

﴿Indeed, We surely help Our messengers and those who believe﴾ ... etc. This is a resumed discourse, directed from Him, the Exalted, to clarify that what befell the disbelievers of the punishment described is among the branches of a universal rule demanded by wisdom, namely that Our constant way is that We help Our messengers and their followers.

﴿in the life of this world﴾ by proof, victory, and avenging them upon the disbelievers through uprooting, killing, taking captives, and other punishments. What may happen to them by way of an appearance of defeat, as a trial, does not detract from this, since consideration is only given to the outcomes and the predominant state of affairs.

﴿and on the day when the witnesses will stand﴾ i.e., the Day of Resurrection. He expressed it thus to indicate the manner of the help, and that it will occur in the presence of all the first and the last, through the testimony of the witnesses for the messengers that they conveyed the message, and against the disbelievers that they denied it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 52:

﴿The Day when their excuse will not benefit the wrongdoers﴾ is a substitute (badal) for the first (phrase, i.e., the "Day" mentioned in the previous verse). The non-benefit of the excuse is because it is void (batilah), and it has been read as: (لا تنفع) with the ta' (i.e., "lā tanfa'u," with a feminine verb form, referring to the excuse).

﴿And theirs is the curse﴾, i.e., distance from mercy.

﴿And theirs is the evil abode﴾, i.e., Jahannam (Hell).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 53:

﴿And We certainly gave Moses the guidance﴾ (al-huda), meaning that by which one is guided, namely the miracles, the scriptures (suhuf) and the laws (shara'i'), ﴿and We caused the Children of Israel to inherit the Book﴾, and We left behind them after him the Torah.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 54:

﴿Guidance and a reminder﴾: as guidance and as a reminder, or as one who guides and one who reminds.

﴿For people of understanding﴾: for those possessed of sound intellects who act upon what is within its folds.

Abu al-Su'ud, Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, on surah 40, verse 55:

﴿So be patient﴾ over what you have suffered from the harm of the polytheists.

﴿Indeed, the promise of Allah﴾ i.e., His promise, which is expressed by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We had already preceded Our word to Our servants, the messengers. Indeed, they would be the ones given victory. And indeed, Our soldiers will be the victorious﴾. Or it means His specific promise to you, or all His promises, of which this is one.

﴿True﴾, admitting no breach at all. He cited the situation of Musa and Fir'awn (p-281) as an example. ﴿And ask forgiveness for your sin﴾, as a making up for what has passed from you of leaving the better course at certain times, for He, Exalted is He, is sufficient for you in supporting your religion and making it prevail over all religion.

﴿And glorify with the praise of your Lord in the evening and the morning﴾: i.e., persist in glorifying, joined with praise of Him, Exalted is He. It is also said: pray for these two times, since the obligatory prayer in Makkah was two rak'ahs in the morning and two rak'ahs in the evening. It is also said: pray in gratitude to your Lord in the evening and the morning. It is also said: they are the Asr prayer and the Fajr prayer.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 56:

﴿Indeed, those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah﴾ and deny them, ﴿without any authority that has come to them﴾ from Him, Exalted is He, concerning that. The restriction of the disputation to this (condition), although the coming of such authority is impossible, is to signal that speaking about matters of religion must absolutely be based on a clear authority. This applies to every false disputant, even though it was revealed concerning the polytheists of Makkah. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿there is nothing in their breasts but pride﴾ is the predicate of "inna" (indeed), meaning: there is nothing in their hearts but arrogance toward the truth and self-magnification against reflection and learning; or nothing but the desire for leadership and preeminence in an absolute sense; or nothing but the desire that prophethood should be theirs rather than yours, out of envy and rebellion, just as they said: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man of the two towns?﴾ and they said: ﴿Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it.﴾ It is for this reason that they dispute concerning them, not that there is any ground for dispute in them, or that they possess something which could be imagined as a basis for disputing in general. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿they will never attain it﴾ is a description of "kibr" (pride). Mujahid said: "They will not attain what that pride entails, which is what they desired of leadership or prophethood." It has also been said: the disputants are the Jews, who used to say, "You are not our companion mentioned in the Torah; rather he is the Messiah son of Dawud," meaning the Dajjal (the Antichrist), who will emerge at the end of time, whose dominion will reach the land and the sea, rivers will flow with him, and he is one of the signs of Allah Exalted; then the kingdom will return to us. So Allah Exalted named their wishing for that "pride," and denied that they would attain what they wished for.

﴿So seek refuge in Allah﴾, that is: take refuge in Him from the plotting of one who envies you and transgresses against you. Within this is an allusion that it (the envy) is among the whisperings of the devils.

﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾ of your sayings and your deeds. His saying, Exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 57:

﴿Surely the creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind﴾ — a confirmation of the truth and a clarification of the most well-known of what they dispute concerning the matter of resurrection, in the same manner as His words, exalted is He: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the like of them?﴾ ﴿But most of mankind do not know﴾ — due to their deficiency in reflection and contemplation, and because of the extent of their heedlessness and their following of their desires.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 58:

﴿And the blind and the seeing are not alike﴾, i.e., the heedless and the one who seeks insight. ﴿Nor are those who believe and do righteous deeds and the evildoer﴾, i.e., the good-doer and the wrongdoer. There must be another state in which the disparity between the two groups will become manifest, and it is what comes after the Resurrection. The particle "lā" ("not") is repeated before "the evildoer" to emphasize the negation, because of the length of the relative clause (al-ṣilah), and because the intended meaning is the negation of the evildoer's equality with the good-doer in the merit and honor that the latter possesses. The second conjunction, joining "those who believe" to what was conjoined to "the blind and the seeing," is for the difference of the two descriptions in what is intended, or for indicating [the point] explicitly and by way of illustration.

﴿Little do you remember﴾, addressed in the second person by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), (p-282) i.e., you remember only a little. It is also read in the third person (ghaybah), and the pronoun refers to the people or to the disbelievers.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 59:

﴿Indeed, the Hour is surely coming; there is no doubt about it﴾ That is: about its coming, due to the clarity of its signs and the consensus of the Messengers upon the promise of its occurrence. ﴿But most of the people do not believe﴾ they do not affirm it, because their insight is confined to the outward appearances of what they perceive through their senses.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 60:

﴿And your Lord says: Call upon Me﴾ i.e., worship Me.

﴿I will respond to you﴾ i.e., I will reward you, in accordance with His saying, exalted is He.

﴿Indeed, those who disdain My worship will enter Hell in humiliation﴾ i.e., abased and debased. And if "supplication" (du'a') is interpreted as "request" (su'al), then the matter that diverts from it is treated as equivalent to disdaining worship, for emphasis. Or the intended meaning of "worship" is supplication, for it is among the best of its forms. And it has been recited as: (sa-yudkhalūna) in the passive form from the causative (al-idkhal, "causing to enter").

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 61:

﴿It is Allah who made the night for you that you may rest therein﴾ by creating it cold and dark, so that it results in the weakening of movements and the quieting of the senses, that you may rest in it. The fronting of the prepositional phrase (al-jar wa-al-majrur, "the prepositional phrase") before the object (al-maf'ul, "the object") has had its rationale (sirr) explained many times before.

﴿And the day as something to see by﴾, i.e., as something seen in or by it. ﴿Indeed, Allah is full of bounty﴾, a great bounty that no other bounty can equal or approach, ﴿to mankind, but most of mankind do not give thanks﴾, due to their ignorance of the Benefactor and their neglect of the places of blessings. The repetition of "mankind" (al-nas) serves to restrict ingratitude (al-kufran) to them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 62:

﴿That is﴾ the One who alone performs the acts that necessitate divinity and lordship, ﴿Allah, your Lord, the Creator of all things. There is no god but Him﴾. These are successive predicates: the latter ones specify the earlier ones and confirm them. It is also read as ( khaliqa ) in the accusative, by way of specification (ikhtisas), so that "there is no god but Him" becomes a resumptive statement (isti'naf) which is, as it were, the conclusion (natijah) drawn from the attributes mentioned.

﴿So how are you turned away?﴾ How, and by what means, are you diverted from worshipping Him alone to worshipping other than Him?

So are those turned away who used to deny the signs of God.
