That is: just as this strange falsehood, which has no basis and no justification at all, turns away everyone who denies the signs of God, of whatever kind they may be, and not some other falsehood that has a basis and some justification in general.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 64:

﴿It is Allah who made the earth a dwelling-place for you, and the sky a canopy﴾. This is an explanation of His favour concerning place, after the explanation of His favour concerning time. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and He shaped you and perfected your shapes﴾ is an explanation of His favour concerning themselves. The "fa" (fa, here) in "fa-ahsana" is explanatory (tafsiriyyah), for the excellence (ihsan) is the very shaping (taswir); that is, He shaped you in the finest shaping, in that He created you upright of stature, fair of skin, well-proportioned in limbs and features, and fitted for practising crafts and acquiring perfections. (p-283)

﴿And He provided you with good things﴾, i.e., delights.

﴿That is⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿ Allah, your Lord﴾: that one who is described by the sublime attributes mentioned, ﴿Allah﴾ and ﴿your Lord﴾ are two predicates of ﴿that﴾. ﴿So blessed is Allah﴾, i.e., exalted in His essence, ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾, i.e., their Owner and their Sustainer. All of them, under His dominion, are in need of Him in their essence, their existence, and all their conditions, such that if His overflowing bounty were cut off from them for a single instant, they would wholly cease to exist.

He is the Living (al-Hayy), the One who alone possesses true, intrinsic life, ﴿there is no god but He﴾, since there is no existent that can approach Him in His essence, His attributes, or His acts.

﴿So call upon Him﴾, that is, worship Him alone, since what necessitates worship is exclusively His, the Exalted ﴿, making your religion sincerely His﴾, i.e., obedience, free from both manifest and hidden shirk.

﴿Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾, i.e., saying this. On the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: Whoever says, "There is no god but Allah," let him follow it immediately by saying, "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds."

﴿Say: Indeed, I have been forbidden to worship those you call upon besides God, since the clear proofs have come to me from my Lord.﴾ These clear proofs are the arguments (*ḥujaj*) and the signs (*āyāt*), or they are the signs, because they confirm the proofs of reason (*adillat al-ʿaql*, the rational proofs) and draw attention to them. The revealed signs (*al-āyāt al-tanzīliyya*) explain the created signs (*al-āyāt al-takwīniyya*), both the outward signs of the horizons (*al-āfāqiyya*) and the inward signs of the selves (*al-anfusiyya*).

﴿And I have been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds.﴾ That is: to be obedient to Him and to devote my religion sincerely to Him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 67:

﴿He it is who created you from dust﴾, that is, within the creation of Adam, upon him be peace, from it, as its verification has been discussed repeatedly.

﴿Then from a drop [of semen]﴾, that is: then He created you, in detailed creation, from a drop, namely semen (maniyy).

﴿Then from a clot [of blood]; then He brings you forth as an infant (tifl)﴾, that is, as infants (atfal). The singular is used to denote the genus, or to denote each individual of its kind.

﴿Then that you may reach your full strength (ashuddakum)﴾. This is a reason for "He brings you forth", coordinated with another reason for it that is suited to it, as if it were said: then He brings you forth as an infant so that you may grow up little by little, then that you may reach your full perfection in strength and intellect. The same applies to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then that you may become elders (shuyukhan)﴾, which may be coordinated with "that you may reach", and it has been read as "shaykhan" (singular), like His saying, exalted is He, "tiflan". ﴿And among you is he who is taken in death before [that]﴾, that is: before the state of old age, after reaching full strength, or before it as well.

﴿And that you may reach﴾ is connected to a verb understood after it, that is: and that you may reach ﴿a specified term (ajalan musamman)﴾, which is the time of death, or the Day of Resurrection, by doing that.

﴿And perhaps you will reason (ta'qilun)﴾: and so that you may comprehend the various kinds of wisdom and lessons contained in that.

He is the One who gives life (ﷺ?) — no, correcting: "He is the One who gives life to the dead and causes the living to die, or the One who does the giving of life and the causing of death."

"And when He decrees a matter" — i.e., He wills a matter among affairs — "then He only says to it, 'Be,' and it is." — without any dependence upon anything at all. This is an illustration of the effect of His power over things that are willed, and a depiction of the swiftness with which created things come into being upon His bringing them into existence, without there being any command-giver and one commanded. The first "fa'" (then) indicates that what follows it is a result of what precedes it, namely the exclusivity of giving life and causing death to Him, glory be to Him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 69:

﴿Have you not seen those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah? How are they turned away?﴾ This is an expression of wonder at their abominable conditions and their feeble opinions, and a preface to what follows of the statement of their denial of the entire Qur'an and all the other scriptures and laws, and the arrangement of the threat upon that. Likewise, what preceded in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah...﴾ . . . etc., is an explanation that their disputation is founded upon a corrupt basis that can hardly enter into existence, namely empty wishful thinking; so there is no repetition in it. That is: look at these obstinate ones who dispute concerning His exalted signs, which are clear, which necessitate belief in them, and which restrain from disputing about them. How are they turned away from them, when the motives to turn toward them are mutually reinforcing and the impediments against them are entirely absent?

And His statement, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 70:

﴿Those who denied the Book﴾ — i.e., all of the Qur'an, or the category of heavenly books. For denying it is a denial of them as well. It is in the genitive position as a substitute (badal) for the first relative clause (al-mawsul al-awwal), or it is in the accusative position, or in the nominative position by way of censure (dhamm). The second relative clause was connected with "denial" rather than "disputation" because disputation customarily occurs concerning some matters and not all of them. The past-tense form is used to indicate certainty, just as the present-tense form in the first relative clause indicates the renewal and repetition of disputation.

﴿and with that which We sent with Our messengers﴾ — from among the other books, or from revelation and laws in general.

﴿Then they will come to know﴾ — the reality (kunh) of what they did of disputation and denial when they witness its punishments.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 71:

﴿When the shackles are around their necks﴾ is an adverbial clause (zarf) governing ﴿they will know﴾, since the meaning is in the future tense (al-istiqbal), while the past form is used because its occurrence is certain.

﴿And the chains﴾ is coordinated (atf) with ﴿the shackles﴾, and the prepositional phrase is in the intended position of being delayed. It has also been said that it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate has been omitted, because the predicate of the first indicates it. It has also been said that the words of the Exalted, ﴿they are dragged﴾, are the predicate with the returning pronoun omitted, meaning: they are dragged with them. According to the first two views, it is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the pronoun in the adverbial clause. It has also been said that it is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) which occurred as an answer to a question arising from the description of their state, as if it were said: "What will their state be after that?" So it was said: "They will be dragged."

﴿In the boiling water﴾. It was also read: (وَالسَّلَاسِلَ يَسْحَبُونَ) with the accusative (naṣb, the case of the object) and a fatḥa on the yāʾ, by fronting the object (taqdīm al-mafʿūl) and coordinating the verbal sentence (al-jumla al-fi'liyya, a sentence beginning with a verb) with the nominal sentence (al-jumla al-ismiyya, a sentence beginning with a noun). It was also read (السَّلَاسِلِ) with the genitive (jarr), taken according to the sense, because His saying ﴿the shackles are around their necks﴾ carries the meaning "around their necks are the shackles," or else there is an implied bāʾ. The reading with it supports this.

﴿Then in the Fire they are kindled﴾, that is, they are burned, from sajr al-tannur (the kindling of the oven, tannur), when one fills it with fuel. From the same root comes al-sajīr, a close friend, as if he were filled with love. The purpose is to show that they are punished with various kinds of punishment and are moved from one kind of torment to another.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 73:**

﴿Then it will be said to them, "Where is that which you used to associate [with Allah]?"﴾

(p-285) ﴿Min dūni Llāh, qālū ḍallū ʿannā﴾ — that is: it will be said to them, and they will say (the verb is in the past form to indicate certainty). "Ḍallū ʿannā" means they have gone astray from us, i.e., they vanished from us, and that was before their gods were joined with them, or they were lost to us, so we did not find what we had expected from them.

﴿Bal lam nakun nadʿū min qablu shayʾan﴾ — that is: rather, it has become clear to us that we were not worshipping anything by worshipping them, since what appeared to us today is that they were not anything of account, like your saying: "I thought him to be something, but he was not."

﴿Kadhālika﴾ — that is: like that severe misguidance ﴿yuḍillu Llāhu l-kāfirīn﴾ — God misguides the disbelievers, when they are not guided to anything that will benefit them in the Hereafter; or, just as their gods went astray from them, He makes them go astray from their gods, so that even if they sought them out, they would not find one another.

That is: the misguidance ﴿is because of what you used to rejoice in on earth﴾, i.e., you were exultant and arrogant.

﴿Without right﴾, which is polytheism and transgression, ﴿and because of what you used to exult in﴾, i.e., you indulged extensively in exultance and insolence. The shift (al-iltifat) to the second person is for emphasis in rebuke.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 76:

﴿Enter the gates of Hell﴾, that is, its seven gates, which have been apportioned for you.

﴿Abiding therein eternally﴾, your eternal abode therein being predetermined.

﴿Wretched is the abode of the arrogant﴾, that is, Hell is the abode of those who were arrogant towards the truth. The expression of their entry as "abode" (mathwa) is because their entry is by way of eternal abiding.

Surah 40, verse 77:

﴿So be patient﴾ until they encounter what has been prepared for them of punishment. ﴿Indeed, the promise of Allah﴾ regarding their punishment ﴿is true﴾, certain without doubt. ﴿And whether We show you﴾ — i.e., if We show you — "mā" is added to emphasize the conditional, which is why the nun (nūn al-tawkīd, the emphatic nun) attaches to the verb; it does not attach with "in" (in, the conditional particle) alone.

﴿some of what We promise them﴾, namely killing and captivity.

﴿Or We cause you to die﴾ before that ﴿then to Us they will be returned﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, where We will requite them for their deeds. This is the response to "natawaffayannaka" (We cause you to die), while the response to "nurayannaka" (We show you) is omitted, as in "fa-dhāka" (that is). It is also permissible that it be a response to it, in the sense: if We punish them during your life, or do not punish them, then We will surely punish them in the Hereafter with the most severe and dreadful punishment, as is indicated by restricting the mention to the return in this context.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 78:

﴿And We have certainly sent messengers before you; of them are those whom We have related to you, and of them are those whom We have not related to you.﴾ It is said: the number of the prophets, upon them be peace, is one hundred and twenty-four thousand, and those whose accounts are mentioned are individuals who can be counted. It is also said: four thousand from the Children of Israel and four thousand from among the rest of mankind.

﴿And it was not for any messenger﴾ i.e., it was not valid nor proper for any messenger from among them.

﴿to bring a sign except by the permission of Allah﴾ For miracles, with their diverse kinds, are gifts from Allah the Exalted, which He distributed among them according to what His will required, founded upon profound wisdoms, like all other allotments. They have no choice in preferring some of them or in independently bringing forth what is proposed from them.

(p-286) ﴿So when the command of Allah comes﴾ with the punishment in this world and the Hereafter, ﴿it is judged with truth﴾ by the salvation of the one who is in the right and his reward, and the destruction of the one who is in falsehood and his punishment.

﴿And there the falsifiers will lose﴾ i.e., at the time of the coming of the command of Allah. "There" is a place-noun used metaphorically for time.

﴿the falsifiers﴾ i.e., those who adhere to falsehood absolutely, so that the stubborn and those who propose signs are included in them primarily.

Allah is the One Who made the cattle (al-an'am) for you. It has been said that this refers specifically to camels, meaning that He created them for your benefit and welfare. His words, Exalted is He, ﴿so that you may ride some of them and eat some of them﴾, are an elaboration of what the lam (of purpose) indicated in summary. The "min" (from) here denotes the starting point (li-ibtida' al-ghaya), and its meaning is that riding and eating begin from them, i.e., that these two activities are connected to them. It has also been said that the "min" is partitive (lil-tab'id), meaning: that you ride some of them and eat some of them. This is not on the basis that each of riding and eating is restricted to a specific part of them, such that the one cannot be connected to what the other is connected to; rather, it is on the basis that every part of them is suitable for each of the two. The change in the noble wording in the second clause is to observe the rhyme (fawasil), together with indicating the primacy of riding.

﴿And for you therein are other benefits﴾ besides riding and eating, such as their milk, their wool, and their hides.

﴿And that you may reach by means of them a need in your breasts﴾ by carrying your loads from one land to another; ﴿and upon them and upon the ship you are carried﴾. It is possible that what is meant here is carrying women and children upon them in a howdah (hawdaj), and this is the secret in separating it from riding and in combining them with the ship in the matter of carrying, because of the complete correspondence between them, so much so that they were called "ships of the land." It has also been said: they are the eight pairs. So the meaning of riding and eating from them is that both apply to all of them, but not in the sense that each of the two may be attached to each of them, nor in the sense that each of the two is restricted to some specific portion of them such that the other cannot be attached to what the other is attached to. Rather, it is in the sense that eating alone is attached to some of them, such as sheep; and both are attached to some of them, such as camels and cattle. The benefits encompass all of them, and reaching a need upon them encompasses cattle.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 81:

﴿And He shows you His signs﴾ — His proofs, which indicate the perfection of His power and the abundance of His mercy.

﴿So which of the signs of God﴾ — that is: so which one of those manifest signs?

﴿will you deny?﴾ — for each one of them is so evident that no one with any degree of intellect would dare to deny it. The word ﴿أيّ﴾ (ayy, "which") is the object governing the verb "deny." The noun "signs" is made grammatically dependent on the Exalted Name (God) in order to cultivate awe and to emphasize the gravity of denying them. The masculine form is the common and widely used one; the feminine form is rare, because the distinction between masculine and feminine applies to nouns (asma') rather than to adjectives (sifat), as in the example "ḥimār" (male donkey) and "ḥimāra" (female donkey), which is an unusual usage. With "ayy," the feminine is even stranger, because of its indefiniteness (ibhām).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 82:

﴿Have they not travelled⦄ That is: they were made to sit, so they did not travel.

﴿in the land, so that they might see how was the end of those who were before them﴾ from the destroyed nations. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They were more numerous than them and greater in power﴾ ... etc. This is a resumed sentence (isti'naf) brought to explain the beginnings of their conditions and their outcomes. ﴿And traces in the land﴾ remaining after them, of buildings, palaces and reservoirs. It has also been said: they are the traces of their footprints in the land, because of the greatness of their crimes. (p-287) ﴿So what they used to earn did not avail them﴾. The first "ma" is either negative or interrogative in the accusative, governed by "aghna" (availed), and the second is either relative or verbal (masdariyya) in the nominative; that is: it did not avail them, or: what thing availed them, what they acquired or their earnings?

﴿So when their messengers came to them with the clear proofs﴾, that is, with the miracles or with the evident signs.

﴿they rejoiced in what knowledge they had﴾. That is, they displayed their joy in it. This refers to what they held of deviant beliefs ('aqa'id, creeds) and refuted doubts (shubah, doubts). Calling these "knowledge" is said in mockery of them. Or it refers to the knowledge of natural philosophy (ṭaba'i', natural sciences), astrology (tanjim), crafts (ṣana'i', skills), and the like. Or it is the knowledge of the prophets, which their messengers had made manifest, so that the meaning of their rejoicing in it is that they laughed at it and mocked it. The Almighty's words support this: ﴿and what they used to mock at encircled them﴾. It has also been said that the rejoicing belongs to the messengers too, for when they witnessed the persistence of their ignorance and the evil of their end, they rejoiced in the knowledge they had been given, which leads to a good end, and they thanked God for it. ﴿And there encircled those who disbelieved the recompense of their ignorance and their mockery.﴾

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 84:

﴿Then when they saw Our might﴾, that is, the severity of Our punishment. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿with a severe punishment﴾ [7:165, ba'is, meaning intense or severe].

﴿They said: "We believe in Allah alone, and we disbelieve in what we used to associate with Him"﴾, meaning the idols.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 40, verse 85:**

﴿So their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our punishment﴾, i.e., at the sight of Our punishment, because acceptance of faith was then impossible. For this reason it was said that "lam yakun" means "lam yasihh" (it was not valid) and "lam yastaqim" (it was not right). The first "fa'" (fa', the connecting particle) expresses the outcome of their multitude and the intensity of their strength, and of what they used to earn, by their supposition that it would avail them. But nothing resulted from it except the non-availing, so in this sense it functions as a result (natijah), even though it is the reverse of the purpose and the opposite of what was sought, as in your saying: "I admonished him, but he did not heed." The second "fa'" is an explanation and detailing of what was left vague and general regarding the non-availing. Such a "fa'" is very common in speech, and its basis is explanation after vagueness and detail after generality. The third "fa'" is merely for sequence (ta'qib), and it makes what follows it a consequence of what precedes it, occurring right after it, because the content of His saying, ﴿When their messengers came to them﴾ . . . etc., is that they disbelieved. So the whole statement is as if it were said: "They disbelieved, then when they saw Our punishment, they believed." The fourth "fa'" is for coordination with "they believed," as if it were said: "They believed, so it did not benefit them," because the beneficial faith is the voluntary faith.

﴿The sunnah of Allah which has already passed among His servants﴾, i.e., Allah, exalted is He, established this as an enduring practice (sunnah) among the servants. The word "sunnat" is among the emphatic verbal nouns (al-masadir al-mu'akkidah).

﴿And the disbelievers were lost there﴾, i.e., at the time of their seeing the punishment, with "hunalika" understood as a noun of place that has been used metaphorically for time, as has already been explained just above.

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-Mu'min, no spirit of a prophet, nor of a truthful one, nor of a martyr, nor of a believer will remain except that it will send blessings upon him and seek forgiveness for him."
